https://www.deccanchronicle.com/nation/p.text: Stepping up India's trade diplomacy on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal held a fresh round of talks with counterparts from Canada, Saudi Arabia and South Korea, as New Delhi pursued trade agreements and greater market access with major partners.Goyal's meeting with Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu focused on negotiations for the India-Canada Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, or CEPA, and the two countries' target of taking bilateral trade to USD 50 billion by 2030."A productive meeting with Mr. Maninder Sidhu, Minister of International Trade of Canada, on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee," Goyal said. "We reviewed the ongoing negotiations for the India-Canada Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), launched by our Prime Ministers in March this year, to take bilateral trade to USD 50 billion by 2030," he said.Goyal stated that the meeting built on his recent discussions with Sidhu in Mumbai."Building on our recent meeting in Mumbai, we reaffirmed our commitment to expediting negotiations and working towards an early conclusion of the agreement," he said. In another bilateral, Goyal met Saudi Arabia's Commerce Minister Majid bin Abdullah Al-Kassabi, with talks centring on negotiations for a free trade agreement between India and the Gulf Cooperation Council."We discussed progress on the India-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) FTA negotiations & explored opportunities to further strengthen trade & investment ties between our two nations," Goyal said. South Korea was also part of Goyal's Milwaukee trade push.He met South Korean Trade Minister Park Jung-Sung, discussing the upgrading of the India-Korea CEPA. The talks covered balanced trade growth and improved market access for Indian agricultural, pharmaceutical and marine products, alongside Korean manufacturing investment in India.These sessions followed a series of bilaterals Goyal held with major trading partners during the Milwaukee gathering. He met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer as India and the United States continued negotiations on an interim trade agreement."Had a productive discussion with USTR Greer towards early conclusion of a mutually beneficial interim agreement under the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement," Goyal said after the meeting, while both also exchanged views on G20 deliberations. Greer separately described his talks with Goyal as "very constructive".Goyal met European Union Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to discuss the India-EU free trade agreement, the Trade and Technology Council, World Trade Organisation reform and G20 priorities. With Brazil's Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira and Minister of Development, Industry, Trade and Services Márcio Fernando Elias Rosa, Goyal discussed the expansion of the India-MERCOSUR Preferential Trade Agreement, alongside sectoral cooperation, investment and coordination at the G20 and WTO. Goyal's meeting with Mexican Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard focused on expanding trade and investment ties, exploring what Goyal described as "huge potential for deeper cooperation". Poland was another focus, as Goyal met Finance and Economy Minister Andrzej Domański to discuss new avenues for strengthening trade and investment, highlighting how an India-EU trade agreement could create opportunities for businesses and deepen bilateral economic cooperation.The Milwaukee meetings brought several major Indian trade negotiations onto a single diplomatic stage, engaging the United States, European Union, Canada, GCC and South Korea, while simultaneously advancing commercial ties with Brazil, Mexico and Poland.

Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA Microsoft Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions Microsoft outage – live updates Ben Quinn and Andrew Gregory Fri 13 Nov 2026 07.51 EST First published on Fri 13 Nov 2026 04.59 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hospitals, GPs and police forces across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage, which is also expected to disrupt schools, businesses and some travel. Key public services battled to get systems back online amid “widespread” and “serious” disruption to NHS services, as staff resorted to using patient’s paper records after being unable to access email and other IT facilities used to deliver healthcare. Downing Street said it was seeking to establish the “full picture” of Microsoft outages and urged the public to follow advice on “alternative ways to get in touch” where services were disrupted. The disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s amid reports of court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they may not be able to rely on digital tickets. Patients getting their prescriptions were also cautioned about possible delays, schools and universities were unable to access emails, and there were reports that ambulance services had been affected by the outage. The problems began late on Thursday afternoon and users have been unable to access many of Microsoft’s most popular services. Thousands worldwide reported they were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook. The Microsoft executive vice-president Charles Lamanna said the outages did not appear to be the result of a cyber-attack. On Friday morning, the firm said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation”, later issuing an update that it was seeing email traffic being gradually restored. NHS staff arriving at work on Friday morning reported being unable to access email, affecting their ability to deliver healthcare in hospitals and surgeries, amid warnings that the outage would be highly disruptive through the day. View image in fullscreen NHS staff arriving at work on Friday morning reported being unable to access email. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA In some cases, staff said they were able to use their phones to access Microsoft Teams, which is heavily relied upon in the healthcare sector, but meetings were having to be cancelled across the board. An NHS England spokesperson said: “Local NHS services are enacting longstanding measures to manage IT outages and ensure critical services and appointments can continue for patients today – including using other IT systems or paper records where possible.” Rachel Harrison, the GMB national secretary, said: “The Microsoft data outage is having a serious impact across ambulance and NHS trusts. Luckily emergency and life-threatening callouts appear to be unaffected.” Pharmacists warned there would be delays in the issuing of some prescriptions as a result of the incident, which disrupted the ability of some pharmacies to communicate with GP practices and patients. View image in fullscreen National Rail warned that people may not be able to access tickets. Photograph: Posed by model; Oscar Wong/Getty Images While there was no early sign of widespread travel disruption, National Rail warned that people may not be able to access tickets that have been emailed to them. “If you’re unable to locate or access your tickets through your email due to this issue, you may still be able to access your tickets by visiting the website or app where you purchased your tickets from and logging into your account,” it said, recommending that passengers do so before travel. The already backlogged court system was hit with juries in some cases being sent home early, or prisoners not being sent to court. At Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, Judge Maurice Greene said staff had been looking for a fax machine earlier in the morning. “I would say sorry but it’s not my fault. It’s Mr [Bill] Gates’s fault,” he told jurors before sending them home, referring to the cofounder of Microsoft, who officially resigned from Microsoft’s board of directors six years ago. Businesses, meanwhile, were braced for the impact of economic damage while the UK’s top financial regulators, the Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority, were hit by the Outlook outage, although a spokesperson for the bank said “all critical operations” were running normally. However, the turmoil comes on the busiest day of the week for mortgage completions and there were also warnings that digital tickets for events could be affected, with Cheltenham racecourse urging visitors to arrive early. Engineers from the government were working with Microsoft to assess the impact of the outage, according to a minister, while the Welsh government said it was putting contingency plans in place. A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister was being kept updated on the situation, while individual departments would be able to rely on contingency plans where necessary. They declined to say whether Downing Street itself had been affected, adding: “There are contingency measures in place at No 10, as there are with all government departments, to ensure that work can go on as usual.” Asked about the effect specifically on the NHS, they said it appeared all clinical and operation systems were working effectively. However, Britain’s minister for defence readiness and industry, Luke Pollard, said earlier in the morning that the Microsoft outage demonstrated the need for “greater resilience” against technology failures. Pollard told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My appetite for disruption when it comes to using my phone is virtually zero. I imagine that’s the case for every one of your listeners, that people want it to work all the time, every time, and we’re seeing more disruption from those tech companies. That’s partly because we’ve become more dependent on technology.” View image in fullscreen Police said the outage was having an impact on people’s ability to report crimes using official websites. Photograph: Alphotographic/Getty Images Police forces across the country, including Britain’s largest, the Metropolitan police, said the outage was having an impact on the ability to report crimes using official websites. Access to Microsoft products used by MPs was also down. A parliamentary spokesperson said: “We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.” School inspections in England were disrupted after Ofsted said it was unable to receive emails, as hundreds of schools, colleges and universities across the UK were affected. The higher education sector was braced to be the hardest hit, with many UK universities relying on Outlook, OneDrive and other Microsoft services for administration and communications, although Teams appears to be functioning for some online meetings.
